runs.text: Deſpejar de todo a vaſilha, caſa, ou outra couſa.

lines.note: Continues the preceding entry: to empty a vessel, house, or other thing completely. The scan supports vaſilha, caſa, and ou outra rather than the garbled OCR; the historical spelling is retained.
Uchiarai denotes washing. The principal forms rǒ and ǒta carry visible carons; their historical long-vowel notation is retained rather than expanded to modern conjugational forms.
Uchiate means hitting the intended target with a thrown object. The gloss begins acertar tirando and continues with the stone example on the next physical row.

runs.text: com pedra, &c. ¶ Item, Cairem os pon-

lines.note: The stone example completes the first sense; the paragraph sign introduces a second sense concerning how the points on dice fall. Pon- continues as tos below, with a printed terminal division mark.

runs.text: tos dos dados à vontade. Vt,

lines.note: The desired points on the dice complete the second gloss. Sai no me wo begins the Japanese example referring to the outcome of a throw; the visibly italic Vt introduces it.

runs.text: Sairão lhe os dados como queria.

lines.note: Uchiateta completes the example: the dice came out as desired. Sairão lhe is retained as the printed historical Portuguese form in this completed, past context.
Uchiawase means matching or fitting two things evenly. The printed principal part ſuru is retained; du- begins Portuguese duas across the row boundary.
As completes duas couſas, the two objects to be matched. This short continuation remains a separate indented physical line.
Uchiauonoqi is the verb for looking upward, here accompanied by a raised head. The unfamiliar uono sequence is legible and is preserved rather than recast into a modern form.

runs.text: a cabeça hum pouco aleuantada, & virada

lines.note: The Portuguese describes the head as slightly raised and turned; cõ on the preceding line abbreviates com. The direction of the turn is completed below.
Pera tras completes the description of looking upward with the head tilted back. The short continuation is indented and is not part of the following riding-ground entry.

runs.text: Rua, ou carreira de caualos que

lines.note: Uchibaba is a riding road or course located inside an enclosure. The relative clause beginning que continues on the next row.
Completes uchibaba as a riding course within a fence or enclosure. The separate grave-like mark over a supports està; the baseline st ligature expansion and the tilde over u in dalgũa are retained.

runs.text: Agulha que ſe mete no corpo baten-

lines.note: This uchibari denotes a needle inserted into the body by tapping. The final baten- begins Portuguese batendo, describing the manner of insertion.
Do completes batendo; uchibari wo utsu is the example of inserting the needle by striking it. A- begins agulha in its Portuguese explanation.
Gulha completes agulha, and aßi means in this manner. It closes the needle sense before the homonymous paper-lining entry.

runs.text: Forro de papel que ſe poem por den-

lines.note: The second uchibari is a paper lining, distinct from the preceding needle. Den- starts dentro, describing where the lining is placed.

The lining is placed inside a box or a kawago container; Cauago is a Japanese container name embedded in the Portuguese explanation. Vchi- begins the example uchibari wo suru across the physical break.
Bariuo ſuru completes uchibari wo suru, applying this paper lining. Por is the printed historical infinitive corresponding to modern pôr.

runs.text: Banhos que ſe tem dentro de caſa

lines.note: Uchiburo denotes baths maintained inside a house. The location inside the home distinguishes this bath term from a public bath.
The baths are for washing the body, completing the domestic-bath definition. This short indented continuation belongs to uchiburo.

runs.text: O interior, ou parte de dentro do

lines.note: Uchikabuto means the inside or inner part of a helmet. The Portuguese object is completed by capacete on the following row.
Capacete completes the helmet gloss. It is the object of do on the previous row, not an independent entry.

Uchikakari describes leaning or resting against something. The r of Vchicacari is abraded but is retained from the aligned OCR after inspection; the supplied principal forms u and atta remain unexpanded. Ar- begins arrimado below.

runs.text: rimado. ¶ Item, per met. Estar enco-

lines.note: Rimado completes arrimado. The figurative extension then describes depending upon someone, with enco- continuing onto the next row; per met. is retained as printed.
Completes the figurative sense of being supported or protected by another person. The printed emparado is retained rather than modernized to amparado.
Uchikachi means to win or prevail. The principal forms tçu and atta accord with the victory sense, first illustrated by warfare.
Winning at a game completes the alternative context for uchikachi. The short gloss remains on its separate indented row.
Uchikakomi means surrounding on every side. The printed circumflex in ôda is retained in this principal part.
The surrounding is done with people or troops, completing the preceding definition. The close spacing of comgente is preserved from the baseline and scan.
The noun uchikake denotes a light, unlined outer garment. The scan supplies the i of ſingela that the OCR omitted; the material follows below.

The garment is of nuno cloth and compared with a dōbuku coat. The mark over o in Dôbucu points upward, supporting a circumflex rather than the OCR tilde; both nuno and Dôbucu occur within the Portuguese explanation.
The verb uchikake first means throwing or laying something upon something else. The principal forms uru and eta are retained as printed.

runs.text: ou vestir ſobre outra ſem ſe cingir. ¶ Itẽ,

lines.note: The clothing sense is putting a garment over another without fastening it with a girdle. The paragraph then introduces a striking or beating sense.
Migiwa no iwa ni nami uchikakuru describes waves striking rocks at the water’s edge. The Japanese verb is physically divided as vchica- / quru.

runs.text: Baterem as ondas na penedia da pra-

lines.note: Quru completes the preceding verb. The Portuguese translation has waves striking the rocky shore, with pra- continued as ya on the next row.
Ya completes praya. Tsubute wo uchikakuru introduces a separate example of throwing stones, whose Portuguese explanation continues below.
Às pedradas completes the stone-throwing sense. The following clause introduces hanging something from an object; the supporting pole or cane is named below.
Pao, ou cana completes the hanging sense: from a stick or cane. The unaccented pao is preserved as printed.
Uchikata here means a married woman, specifically the wife of an ordinary man. It begins a new unindented headword line; the OCR indentation is corrected.
Uchikayeshi means turning something upward from below. The scan reads baixo, correcting OCR buixo; the printed principal part eita is retained as the dictionary’s historical form.
Rà completes perà: turning from below upward. The baseline grave accent is retained after reinspection of the faint mark above a, rather than normalized to unaccented pera.
Uchichigaye describes striking one another. The reciprocal action is explained with weapons on the next row; this is an unindented entry start.

runs.text: tro com Catana, ou montante, ou matarenſe.

lines.note: Completes the reciprocal sense: striking with a katana or two-handed sword, or killing one another. Catana is the Japanese sword name within the Portuguese sentence.

runs.text: ¶ Itẽ, Atraueſar hũa couſa ſobre outra como a

lines.note: A second sense is crossing one thing over another. The following row supplies garments whose sides cross; Atraueſar is retained with the printed single long s.

The examples are a stole and a Japanese quimão garment. Enlargement supports estola, correcting OCR eclola: the worn low s is distinct from the following tall t. Quimão and Iapão retain their Portuguese spellings.
Uchikomi means driving something inside by striking it. The definition continues at the top of the second column with the nail example; this entry start is unindented.
Continues uchikomi from the first column with the example of driving a nail. Kugi wo hashira ni begins the Japanese phrase, specifying a nail and a pillar.
Uchikomu completes the phrase about driving a nail into a pillar. Faxira, the Japanese word for pillar, appears inside the Portuguese explanation and is retained with its printed capital.
Tsubute wo uchikomu is throwing a stone into an interior. Atirando com begins its Portuguese explanation, continued below.

runs.text: pedra metela dentro dalgũa caſa. ¶ Item,

lines.note: Completes the action of throwing a stone into a house. A following Item introduces another sense of uchikomu; the final comma is visible in the scan.
The repeated uchikomu introduces the figurative sense of being lodged within someone’s heart or affections. It is an indented continuation of the entry, not a new column-level headword.
Sono hito ni uchikonda illustrates becoming deeply attached to that person. The printed division after vchicô is a hyphen, not the OCR full stop.

runs.text: Terſe feito hũa couſa, ou muito amigo,

lines.note: Da completes the preceding past form. The Portuguese describes becoming as one with someone or becoming a close friend; its final characterization continues below.

The first clause completes the intimate-friend sense. The next example concerns staking possessions at gambling; the damaged spaced Z ifôuo is retained provisionally, probably intended as zaifō wo, rather than supplying an invisible a.

runs.text: Iugar, ou meter no jogo o

lines.note: Ni uchikomu completes the gambling construction. Portuguese Iugar, ou meter no jogo means gambling or putting possessions into the game; Iugar is retained as the printed vowel spelling.
Fato and fazenda complete the property at stake in the gambling example: goods and wealth. This short continuation belongs to the preceding verb entry.
Uchikoroshi means killing by blows. The principal part oita is the historical s-verb form supplied by the dictionary and is not modernized to oshita.

runs.text: ou às pedradas, ou com eſpada.

lines.note: The alternatives are killing by stones or by a sword. The scan shows separate ou às, correcting the OCR run-together ouas.
Uchikoshi means passing over or crossing. Yama- begins the mountain example; the printed hyphen is kept even though the break falls before the following object particle.
Yama wo uchikosu means crossing mountains. The Portuguese repeats the crossing sense, with the locally printed long-s pair retained in Paſſar.
Uchikukumi, also uchikukumi mono, introduces a kind of sword construction. The lowercase l is the alternative-form marker; Cata- begins the sword name across the physical line break.

runs.text: na feita de maneira que o aço fique cuberto, &

lines.note: Na completes Catana. The sword is made so that its steel is covered; the enclosing material and both sides are explained on the next line.

runs.text: como forrado dambas as partes de ferro.

lines.note: The sword’s steel is described as enclosed on both sides by iron. This completes the construction introduced under uchikukumi mono without imposing modern metallurgical terminology.
The verb uchikukumi first means holding something inside the mouth. Its third principal part visibly carries a caron in ǔda; al- begins algũa below.

runs.text: gũa couſa. ¶ Item, Forrar algũa couſa por

lines.note: After completing the mouth sense, Item introduces covering an object on its surface. The last word is por, correcting OCR per; por cima continues below.

runs.text: cima como as guardas da Catana de metal cu-

lines.note: The covering sense is illustrated by metal sword guards. Cu- begins cubertas, describing their coating on the next row; Catana is embedded within the Portuguese explanation.
The guards are covered with gold or silver. Vchi- begins the example uchikukumi ni suru on the following line.
Uchikukumi ni suru means lining or plating something. The Portuguese introduces applying a metal layer, with the object continued below.

runs.text: couſa de algum metal ſobre outro.

lines.note: Completes the plating explanation as one metal laid over another. It closes the covering sense of uchikukumi.
Uchikudaki means breaking something into pieces. The principal part aita reflects the supplied historical conjugation; the synonym eſmiuçar follows on the next row.
After the literal breaking sense, per met. introduces speaking plainly or intimately. Uchikudaite kata- begins the example with the historical te-form of uchikudaku.
Ru completes kataru: speaking familiarly without leaving anything out. The final na begins nada on the next row; its a is visible at the curved column edge, with no secure terminal hyphen.
Da completes nada, making the explanation “leaving nothing untold.” The short continuation closes the figurative speaking example.
Uchikurubushi is the ankle bone on the inner side. The scan gives dentro, correcting the OCR dentmro, and a final punctuation dot is retained.
Tokurubushi supplies the contrasting outer ankle bone. This indented paired term follows the inner-ankle definition and is not a Japanese word embedded within Portuguese.
Uchidashi means sending out or bringing into view, here concerning enemies or troops. Aparecer is legible at the curved edge and corrects OCR apareur.

runs.text: como inimigos, ou gẽte de guerra. Vt,

lines.note: The illustrative setting is enemies or military forces. The Japanese begins Teqiga, “the enemy,” with the subject particle attached; the scan supports qi rather than the OCR u.

Ninjū wo uchidasu completes the enemy’s deployment of troops. The gloss says to bring them out or show them. Darmostras retains the close printed spacing; st is the provisional local expansion of the same looped ligature seen in esta/Estar, recovered here from garbled OCR.

runs.text: da gẽte de guerra. ¶ Itẽ, Ganhar, ou auerjugã

lines.note: After completing the deployment of troops, the entry adds obtaining or winning through gambling. The compressed auerjugã continues with do below: jugãdo is the printed gerund, and the tilde over a supplies the nasal abbreviation.
Do completes jugãdo. Ano hito wa bakuchi de takara wo begins the example of a man acquiring wealth by gambling; the final object particle uo is visible at the curved edge.

runs.text: Aquelle homẽ com o jogo dosda-

lines.note: Uchidaita completes the past-tense example. The Portuguese says that man won goods or wealth at dice; the visible terminal mark after dosda- divides dados across the row boundary.
Dos completes dados, followed by the goods or property won. The Portuguese ganhou agrees with the completed Japanese action in uchidaita.

runs.text: Aparte da Catana com que ſe corta, q̃

lines.note: Uchido denotes the cutting portion of a katana. The final q̃ is visible beside the curved rule and introduces the relative clause below; the OCR omitted it.

runs.text: he entre o meo, & o cabo.

lines.note: The cutting portion is described as lying between the middle and the end. The source’s wording is retained without imposing a modern technical subdivision of the blade.

runs.text: Deſpojos que hum toma na guerra ao

lines.note: Uchidori denotes spoils taken in war from someone one has killed. The final ao is visible and completes the required Portuguese relation with que matou below.
After completing the slain-opponent definition, uchidori kōmyō shite begins an example combining taking spoils with gaining renown. Both long-o marks in cǒmeǒ point downward and remain carons.
The example means taking spoils and acquiring a name and fame. The legible final fa begins fama below; the curved edge does not supply a secure hyphen, so none is invented.
Ma completes fama. Uchidori ni shita katana ja, printed as Vchidorini xita catanagia, says this is a sword taken as spoil; Esta begins its Portuguese translation.

runs.text: Catana tomei por deſpojos da guerra aos ini-

lines.note: The Portuguese says this katana was taken as war booty from enemies. Ini- begins inimigos, with a visible division mark at the bent right edge.
Migos completes inimigos and closes the war-spoils example. The continuation is brief but is a separate physical body row.

Uchidōshi denotes the long iron blade of a naginata. The faint d in comprido and the compressed final letters of Naguinata are read from the scan; Naguinata is a Japanese weapon name inside the Portuguese gloss.
Uchiharai means shaking off or throwing out. The scan reads fora, correcting OCR ſoru, and both principal-form o marks are carons.

Chiri wo uchiharō illustrates shaking off dust. Portuguese opoo preserves the close printed article-plus-noun spacing and unaccented oo; pa- begins palhas, which continues on f533. The isolated lhas below is the catchword and is recorded separately.
The isolated bottom-right catchword anticipates lhas at the opening of f533, completing the divided pa- / lhas. It is page furniture rather than a second occurrence in the running definition.
